subject: EVS Part 1
notes: India is a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides – the Arabian Sea to the west, the Bay of Bengal to the east and the Indian Ocean to the south.
The northern border of India is the Himalayan mountain range, the highest peaks reaching over 8,000 m.
Major rivers flow from the Himalayas to the plains and then to the sea: Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra, Godavari, Narmada, Krishna, Kaveri and others.
Rivers have a slope – they flow downhill from high to low places. The slope is steeper in the mountains and gentler in the plains.
Plateaus are flat elevated areas; the Deccan Plateau covers most of southern India.
Deserts are found in the north‑west (Thar Desert) and in the central part (Bikaner Desert).
India has many islands: Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea, Andaman and Nicobar in the Bay of Bengal, and several coastal islands along the Konkan coast.
The capital of India is New Delhi, located in the northern part of the country.
Rajasthan is the largest state by area, followed by Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.
The smallest state is Goa, and the smallest union territory is Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
The Great Indian Desert (Thar) lies mainly in Rajasthan.

Cash crops such as tea, coffee, saffron, cloves, apples and oranges are grown in specific states – e.g., tea in Assam, coffee in Karnataka, saffron in Himachal Pradesh, apples in Himachal and Uttarakhand, oranges in Maharashtra.
Transport routes on the map show how goods move between states – e.g., a route from Nagpur to Bikaner for oranges.
The Indian subcontinent has diverse climates, leading to varied crops: wheat in the north, rice in the south, jowar in the central plains.
India’s cultural diversity includes many languages, religions, castes, festivals, clothing and food traditions.
The political map shows states, union territories, capitals and important cities; the map also indicates the largest state in yellow and the state in the user’s home state in a favourite colour.
The map also shows the names of rivers, mountains, plateaus, deserts, gulfs and islands, and their directions of flow or location.
Students should learn to read a map, identify features, and answer questions about them.
Key terms: peninsula, Himalayas, plateau, desert, river basin, capital, union territory, cash crop, transport route.

quiz.explain: The Bay of Bengal is on the eastern side of India.

quiz.explain: Rajasthan is the largest state in India.

quiz.q: Which of the following islands is part of the Andaman and Nicobar group?
quiz.explain: Port Blair is the capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

quiz.q: The Ganga River flows through which of these states?
quiz.explain: The Ganga flows mainly through Uttar Pradesh.

quiz.q: Which of these crops is primarily grown in the northern plains of India?
quiz.explain: Wheat is a main crop in northern India.

quiz.q: The Arabian Sea is located to the ___ of India.
quiz.explain: The Arabian Sea lies to the west of India.

quiz.q: Which river is known as the 'Sister River' of the Ganga?
quiz.explain: The Yamuna is called the sister river of the Ganga.

quiz.q: Which of the following states is the smallest by area in India?
quiz.explain: Goa is the smallest state by area.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: - A house is a shelter that protects us from sun, wind, rain and cold.
- Houses are built using materials that are available locally – wood, stone, earth, bricks, cement, glass, metal, tin sheets, etc.
- The shape of a house (rectangular, square, round) and its roof type (flat, sloping, thatched) depend on the climate and the region.
- In plains with moderate rainfall, houses are usually rectangular with stone or earth walls and a sloping roof made of thatch or tiles.
- In heavy rainfall areas, houses have steep roofs to shed rainwater and walls made of earth or stone to keep the interior dry.
- In desert regions, houses are built with thick walls of earth or mud to keep the interior cool and roofs are flat or low sloping.
- In marshy or wetland areas, houses are raised on stilts or made of bamboo to avoid flooding.
- In mountainous regions, houses are small, low‑profile, often made of stone or wood, with steep roofs to handle snow and wind.
- Eco‑friendly houses use renewable energy (solar, wind, biogas), recycle water and waste, avoid artificial colours, and allow natural light and ventilation.
- Pollution from construction (dust, noise, chemical runoff) can harm the environment and people nearby.
- Homeless people lack basic needs like shelter, water, food and education; governments try to provide shelters and housing schemes.
- Children can help by making models of eco‑friendly houses, preparing street plays, and raising awareness about pollution and energy use.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a house?
quiz.explain: A house shelters us from sun, wind, rain and cold.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used for walls in plains?
quiz.explain: Plains houses often use stone or earth walls.

quiz.q: Which roof type is suitable for heavy rainfall areas?
quiz.explain: Steep roofs shed rainwater quickly.

quiz.q: What is a key feature of eco‑friendly houses?
quiz.explain: They use renewable energy like solar or wind.

quiz.q: Which region uses houses built on stilts?
quiz.explain: Stilt houses avoid flooding in wetland areas.

quiz.q: What is a major source of pollution at construction sites?
quiz.explain: Construction creates noise, dust, and water pollution.

quiz.q: Which material is NOT typically used for building walls in mountainous houses?
quiz.explain: Plastic is rarely used in traditional mountain houses.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of using solar panels in a house?
quiz.explain: Solar panels provide free energy, reducing bills.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a reason for building houses differently in each region?
quiz.explain: All factors influence house design.

quiz.q: What is a common practice to protect homeless people?
quiz.explain: Shelters provide basic protection for homeless.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: - Food is the energy that keeps us alive and growing.
- Plants make food by photosynthesis using sunlight, water and air.
- Seeds are the starting point of a new plant; improved seeds give higher yield and resist pests.
- Two main seasons for farming in India: Kharif (June‑October) and Rabi (October‑March).
- Modern irrigation methods: drip irrigation (drops water near roots) and sprinkle irrigation (sprays water over the field).
- Fertilizers give extra nutrients; natural fertilizers are manures, chemical fertilizers are artificial.
- Overuse of chemical fertilizers can lower soil fertility and harm the environment.
- Storing grain in dry, airy places prevents insects and fungus.
- Food security means every person gets enough food; laws and programmes help farmers and consumers.
- Green Revolution increased food production through better seeds and technology.
- Organic farming uses natural materials and keeps soil healthy.
- Farmers use modern tools like tractors, improved seeds, and irrigation to increase yield.
- Storage of food by animals (ants, bees, squirrels) shows nature’s way of keeping food safe.

quiz.q: Which season in India is called the kharif season?
quiz.explain: Kharif season is from June to October, mainly rainfed.

quiz.q: What is the main source of water for rabi crops?
quiz.explain: Rabi crops rely on rainwater, monsoon runoff, and dew.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method drips water only near the roots?
quiz.explain: Drip irrigation delivers water close to plant roots.

quiz.q: What is a natural fertilizer called?
quiz.explain: Natural fertilizer is called organic manure.

quiz.q: Which crop is grown in the summer season?
quiz.explain: Jowar (sorghum) is a summer crop.

quiz.q: Which of these is a modern method of irrigation?
quiz.explain: Sprinkle irrigation is a modern method.

quiz.q: What happens if chemical fertilizers are overused?
quiz.explain: Overuse reduces soil fertility.

quiz.q: Which of these is a pest that spoils stored grain?
quiz.explain: Mice can damage stored grain.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of storing grain in a dry place?
quiz.explain: Dry storage prevents fungus and insects.

quiz.q: Which scientist is credited with the Green Revolution in India?
quiz.explain: Dr. M.S. Swaminathan led the Green Revolution.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Drying removes water to stop micro‑organism growth.
Cooling in a refrigerator keeps food at low temperature so bacteria cannot multiply.
Boiling destroys bacteria and fungi by high heat.
Canning seals food in airtight containers to prevent air and microbes from entering.
Adding preservatives like salt, sugar, vinegar, or spices stops spoilage by creating hostile conditions.
Spices can be dried and stored for long periods because they contain natural preservatives.
Food should be kept away from moisture, heat, and insects to avoid spoilage.
Micro‑organisms need food, water, warmth, and air to grow.
Proper cleaning of utensils and hands prevents contamination.
Storing food in the right season (e.g., drying in summer) helps preserve it for the whole year.
Chilled milk stays fresh longer because cold slows bacterial activity.
Fruits and vegetables spoil faster in warm, humid conditions; they last longer when kept cool.
Preservatives work by lowering water activity or changing pH to inhibit microbes.
A closed jar with a cloth cover allows fermentation while preventing contamination.
Food that shows mold, foul smell, or color change should be discarded.

quiz.q: Which method removes water from food to stop microbes from growing?
quiz.explain: Drying removes water, which microbes need to grow.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of adding salt to food?
quiz.explain: Salt creates a dry environment that kills or stops microbes.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a method of food preservation mentioned?
quiz.explain: Freezing was not listed in the chapter.

quiz.q: Why do we avoid eating food that has started to grow fungus?
quiz.explain: Fungus can cause illness.

quiz.q: What does a refrigerator do to food?
quiz.explain: Refrigeration keeps food cold, slowing microbes.

quiz.q: Which substance is NOT mentioned as a preservative?
quiz.explain: Mustard oil was not listed; the chapter mentioned salt, sugar, vinegar.

quiz.q: When should fruits be stored to keep them fresh for a long time?
quiz.explain: Refrigeration keeps fruits fresh longer.

quiz.q: What is the main reason for keeping food in an airtight container?
options: To stop air and microbes from entering
quiz.explain: Airtight containers prevent microbes from entering.

quiz.q: Which of these is a type of drying method?
quiz.explain: Papads are dried to preserve them.

quiz.q: What happens to food if it is left at room temperature for several days?
options: It may develop fungus and spoil
quiz.explain: Room temperature encourages microbial growth.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Transport is the movement of people or goods from one place to another.
There are three main types of transport: land, water and air.
Land transport includes walking, bicycles, motor vehicles and trains.
Water transport uses boats, ships and barges to carry goods and passengers.
Air transport uses aeroplanes and helicopters to travel over long distances.
Walking is the simplest and most eco‑friendly way to travel short distances.
Bicycles are good for short to medium distances and give physical exercise.
Motor vehicles (cars, buses, autorickshaws) use fuel and can travel faster but produce pollution.
Trains are efficient for long distances and can carry many passengers or goods at once.
Ships are used for long sea journeys and can carry huge amounts of cargo.
Airplanes are the fastest way to travel long distances but consume a lot of fuel.
Transport saves time and effort, making work and trade easier.
Different modes of transport have advantages and disadvantages.
Using public transport reduces traffic and pollution compared to private cars.
Bicycles produce no pollution and are good for health and environment.
Walking and cycling help keep the air cleaner and reduce noise pollution.
Transport connects distant places, making the world feel closer.
Fuel burning in vehicles releases carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide and sulphur dioxide.
Air pollution harms plants, animals and human health, causing respiratory problems.
To reduce pollution, use public transport, walk or cycle whenever possible, and maintain vehicles properly.

quiz.q: Which mode of transport takes the longest time for a short distance?
quiz.explain: Walking is the slowest mode of transport.

quiz.q: What is a main cause of air pollution from vehicles?
quiz.explain: Vehicles emit carbon monoxide, a harmful gas.

quiz.q: Which transport mode is most fuel efficient for short trips?
quiz.explain: Bicycles do not use fuel.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of transport?
quiz.explain: Pollution is a drawback, not a benefit.

quiz.q: Which vehicle is best for carrying small loads and reduces crowding?
quiz.explain: Bicycles can carry small loads and reduce crowding.

quiz.q: What does CNG stand for?
quiz.explain: CNG means Compressed Natural Gas.

quiz.q: Which transport option is recommended for a grandmother who gets tired easily?
quiz.explain: A bus provides comfortable seating for the elderly.

quiz.q: Which gas is NOT mentioned as a pollutant from vehicles?
quiz.explain: Oxygen is not listed as a pollutant.

quiz.q: Which activity helps reduce noise pollution?
quiz.explain: Public transport reduces the number of vehicles, lowering noise.

quiz.q: Which of these is a remedy to reduce pollution from transport?
options: Using fuels that cause less pollution
quiz.explain: Using cleaner fuels helps reduce pollution.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: - Communication is the exchange of information between people.
- Mass media are tools like TV, radio, newspapers, internet that reach many people at once.
- Artificial satellites help send TV programmes and mobile phone signals across the world.
- Telecommunication means talking to someone far away using phones or the internet.
- Advantages of mass media: easy contact, saves time, raises awareness, warns about disasters, supports government schemes, helps trade and industry.
- Disadvantages: eye, ear and back problems from too much TV, psychological issues, isolation, neglect of outdoor activities.
- TV and mobile phones can be used responsibly to avoid health problems.
- Before phones, messages were sent by letters, telegrams or face‑to‑face talk.
- Audio‑visual communication lets us see the person we talk to on a phone or video call.
- Mass media can educate people about science, health, environment and social issues.

quiz.q: What helps TV programmes reach people in different parts of the world?
quiz.explain: Satellites broadcast TV signals to many places.

quiz.q: Which device lets you talk to someone far away?
quiz.explain: Mobile phones use radio waves to connect distant people.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of watching too much television?
quiz.explain: Excessive TV can cause eye strain and other health issues.

quiz.q: Mass media can warn people about which of these?
quiz.explain: TV and radio can give early warnings of storms, floods, etc.

quiz.q: Before phones, how were long‑distance messages sent?
quiz.explain: Letters and telegrams were used before telephones.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a benefit of mass media?
quiz.explain: Causing eye strain is a disadvantage, not a benefit.

quiz.q: What does the term 'audio‑visual communication' mean?
options: Seeing the person you talk to
quiz.explain: It lets you see the person while you talk, like video calls.

quiz.q: Which device uses satellites to send signals?
quiz.explain: Mobile phones use satellite signals for calls and data.

quiz.q: Mass media helps in the expansion of which sector?
quiz.explain: All listed sectors benefit from mass media.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of using mass media for government schemes?
quiz.explain: Mass media spreads information about schemes to the public.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Water is a liquid that covers most of Earth’s surface and is essential for life.
Water can be clean or polluted. Clean water is safe to drink; polluted water contains harmful substances.
Waste water is water that has been used in homes, factories, or farms and contains dirt, chemicals, or germs.
Sewage is a type of waste water that comes from toilets, kitchens, and bathrooms.

Water is purified before it is supplied to homes. The main steps are: 1) Settling (letting dirt fall to the bottom), 2) Filtration (passing water through sand or charcoal), 3) Chlorination (adding chlorine to kill germs).
Oxygen is added to water in water‑works so fish and other aquatic life can breathe. This is called oxygenation.
Rainwater can be collected in clean containers. Rain that falls directly on the ground is usually cleaner than rain that runs over soil or roofs.
If a lot of dirty water is dumped into rivers or lakes, the water becomes polluted and can hurt plants, animals and people.
Water that has no oxygen is bad for fish and other living things in rivers and lakes.
Water‑works use large tanks, filters and chemicals to make water safe for drinking.
When it rains, the water that falls on roofs can be stored in tanks or let seep into the ground. This helps keep water available during dry seasons.
Water management means collecting, storing or letting water seep into the ground so that it can be used even when it does not rain.
Drought happens when there is very little rain for a long time. It can lead to famine if people and animals do not have enough water.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of treating sewage water before it is released into a water body?
quiz.explain: Treating sewage removes harmful germs and pollutants so the water can be safely used.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a natural purification process for river water?
quiz.explain: Chlorination is a human-made process; the others happen naturally.

quiz.q: In the simple bottle filter experiment, which material is added first?
quiz.explain: The water is poured first, then powdered coal, fine sand, and finally coarse sand.

quiz.q: What happens to the dissolved oxygen level when a lot of waste is added to a river?
quiz.explain: More waste reduces the amount of dissolved oxygen, harming aquatic life.

quiz.q: Which of these is a method of storing rainwater for use after the rainy season?
quiz.explain: All listed methods help store rainwater.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of drinking untreated polluted water?
quiz.explain: Polluted water can carry germs that spread diseases.

quiz.q: Why do we need to crush and throw away empty water bottles?
quiz.explain: Crushing bottles prevents them from being reused and reduces litter.

quiz.q: What is the role of alum in water purification?
quiz.explain: Alum helps particles settle during the settling process.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a step in the water purification process at water-works?
quiz.explain: Evaporation is not part of the purification steps listed.

quiz.q: What is the main effect of not having rain for a long time?
quiz.explain: Long dry periods lead to drought and famine.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Clothes are items we wear to protect our body and give us comfort.
We wear different clothes for different occasions like school, festivals, parties and sports.
Children usually wear simple cotton shirts and trousers, while adults wear shirts, skirts, trousers, sarees or kurtas.
In hot weather we wear light, loose clothes made of cotton or linen.
In cold weather we wear warm clothes like woolen sweaters, jackets and shawls.
Clothes can be made from natural fibres like cotton, wool, silk or from synthetic fibres like polyester and nylon.
The process of making cloth involves: raw material (cotton, wool), spinning, weaving or knitting, dyeing and finishing.
Textile industry is a big part of Maharashtra’s economy; famous products include Paithani saree, Himroo shawl, Solapur bedsheets and Ichalkaranji handloom cloth.
People’s need for clothes is different from their desire for clothes; we need clothes for protection but may want more for fashion or status.
Clothes change with time, culture and climate; traditional clothes vary across states like Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Kerala and Jammu & Kashmir.
When we choose clothes, we should think about the purpose, comfort, and the season.
It is good to borrow or lend clothes to friends when we have extra, but we should keep enough for ourselves.
Advertisements often show many clothes that we do not need; we should be careful not to buy just because they look good.
The raw material for cotton cloth comes from cotton plants; for wool cloth it comes from sheep’s fleece.
Workers in textile industry include spinners, weavers, dyers, and machine operators; they come from many parts of the country.
Textile factories have changed from handloom to powerloom and now to computer‑controlled machines.
Clothes made from natural fibres are usually more breathable and comfortable in hot weather.
Synthetic fibres are strong, wrinkle‑free and easy to wash, but may not be breathable in hot weather.
The choice of clothes should match the climate, activity and the person’s body size.
Traditional clothes of a region reflect its climate, culture and available natural resources.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason people want clothes that they do not need?
quiz.explain: People want clothes for protection, not for desire or greed.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of clothes in different climates?
quiz.explain: Clothes protect us from weather conditions.

quiz.q: Which activity asks students to write the total number of clothes they have?
options: Write the total number of clothes
quiz.explain: The activity instructs to write the total number of clothes.

quiz.q: In the chapter, what is a common source of raw material for fabric?
quiz.explain: Cotton is a common raw material for fabric.

quiz.q: Which season is mentioned as the main time for using certain textiles?
quiz.explain: Textiles are used in all seasons.

quiz.q: What does the chapter suggest about advertising and clothes?
options: It helps people buy necessary clothes
It creates desire for unnecessary clothes
It reduces the need for clothes
quiz.explain: Advertising can create desire for unnecessary clothes.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of traditional saree mentioned?
quiz.explain: Tartan is not listed among the traditional sarees.

quiz.q: What is the main reason Mumbai became a textile hub?
quiz.explain: Mumbai’s humid weather facilitated cloth production.

quiz.q: Which question asks students to consider lending clothes to friends?
options: Do you think you should have other clothes?
Will you lend your clothes to your friends?
How many times do you change clothes?
What do you wear to functions?
quiz.explain: The question explicitly asks about lending clothes.

quiz.q: Which activity involves visiting a local Khadi Gramodyog centre?
options: Make a note of clothes to wear on a traditional day
Visit your local Khadi Gramodyog centre
quiz.explain: The activity mentions visiting a Khadi Gramodyog centre.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Forests are large groups of trees that give homes to many animals and plants.
Trees absorb carbon dioxide and give out oxygen – they help keep the air clean.
When forests are cut down (deforestation) the soil becomes loose and can wash away, causing floods.
Water in rivers and lakes can become dirty if factories dump waste water into them – this is water pollution.
Air pollution happens when factories, cars and power plants release smoke and gases into the air.
Animals that live in forests need trees for food, shelter and protection; if trees disappear they may die or move away.
Plants and animals are called biodiversity; it means many different kinds of living things in one place.
If biodiversity is lost, the whole food chain can break and some animals may become extinct.
Recycling and using less energy can help keep the environment healthy.
India has special places called national parks, wildlife sanctuays and biodiversity parks to protect animals and plants.

quiz.q: What happens to the soil when forests are cut down?
options: It becomes loose and can wash away
quiz.explain: Without tree roots, soil loses structure and can be washed away by rain.

quiz.q: Which gas is released when we burn fuels like petrol and diesel?
quiz.explain: Combustion of fuels produces carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: What is the main reason for water pollution in rivers near factories?
quiz.explain: Factories often release untreated waste water into rivers.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of air pollution?
quiz.explain: Planting trees helps clean the air, not pollute it.

quiz.q: What is a biodiversity park?
options: A park with only one type of tree
A park that protects many kinds of plants and animals
quiz.explain: It is a protected area where many species live.

quiz.q: Which of these animals is likely to move away if forests disappear?
quiz.explain: All listed animals depend on forests for shelter.

quiz.q: What does recycling help to reduce?
quiz.explain: Recycling reduces waste that can cause pollution.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a natural component of the environment?
quiz.explain: River water is a natural, not man‑made, component.

quiz.q: What is migration?
options: Moving from one place to another for food or shelter
quiz.explain: Migration is when animals move to find better conditions.

quiz.q: Which action helps protect the environment?
quiz.explain: Planting trees helps restore forest cover.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: - Food is a substance that gives us energy and helps us grow.
- The main parts of food are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals.
- Carbohydrates are found in rice, wheat, potatoes and give energy.
- Proteins are found in pulses, milk, eggs and help build and repair body tissues.
- Fats are found in oil, butter, nuts and give extra energy and protect organs.
- Vitamins are small amounts of substances (A, B, C, D, E, K) that keep us healthy.
- Minerals are tiny elements (iron, calcium, sodium, potassium) needed for many body functions.
- Fibre is a type of carbohydrate that is not digested and helps food move through the gut.
- A balanced diet contains all these parts in the right amounts.
- If we miss any part for a long time we may become malnourished or develop diseases.
- Eating fruits with skins, whole grains and pulses gives us fibre and micronutrients.
- Milk is given to children daily because it supplies protein, calcium and vitamins.

quiz.q: Which food gives us the most energy?
quiz.explain: Fats give the most energy per gram.

quiz.q: What is the main function of fibre in food?
options: Help food move through the gut
quiz.explain: Fibre helps food move through the digestive system.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is important for good vision?
quiz.explain: Vitamin A prevents night blindness.

quiz.q: What does a balanced diet contain?
quiz.explain: Balanced diet has all nutrients.

quiz.q: Which food is a good source of protein?
quiz.explain: Milk contains protein.

quiz.q: What are micronutrients?
options: Small amounts of vitamins and minerals
quiz.explain: Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a carbohydrate?
quiz.explain: Protein is not a carbohydrate.

quiz.q: Why do we need fats in our diet?
options: They are a type of vitamin
They are a type of mineral
quiz.explain: Fats give energy and protect organs.

quiz.q: What is malnutrition?
options: Eating only one type of food for a long time
quiz.explain: Malnutrition is not getting all nutrients for a long time.

quiz.q: Which part of the body stores excess energy?
quiz.explain: The liver stores excess energy as fat.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Earth rotates around its own axis once every 24 hours – this is called rotation.
The line about which Earth turns is the axis of rotation, passing through the North and South Poles.
The equator is the imaginary circle that divides Earth into northern and southern hemispheres.
Daytime occurs when a part of Earth faces the Sun; nighttime when it faces away.
A full rotation of Earth gives one day, which is divided into 24 hours.
Earth also revolves around the Sun once every 365 days and 6 hours – this is one year.
Because Earth’s axis is tilted, the length of day and night changes with seasons.
The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west because Earth rotates from west to east.
The Moon revolves around Earth once every 28–30 days, producing its phases.
The Moon’s phases are called the waxing (Shukla Paksha) and waning (Krishna Paksha) periods.
A lunar month is the time from one new moon to the next, about 29–30 days.
The month is divided into 15 days of waxing and 15 days of waning, called tithis.
Leap year adds an extra day (29 Feb) every four years to keep the calendar in sync with Earth’s orbit.
The equator is the widest part of Earth, equidistant from the poles.
The North Pole is the point where the axis points north; the South Pole points south.
The Earth’s axis is inclined at about 23.5°, causing seasons.
Sunrise and sunset occur when the Sun crosses the horizon at a particular location.
The Sun rises in the east because Earth’s rotation is anti‑clockwise when viewed from the North Pole.
The Moon is visible only when illuminated by the Sun’s light.
During a full moon, the entire near side of the Moon faces Earth.
During a new moon, the near side is dark and not visible from Earth.
The length of day is longer than night in the Northern Hemisphere between 22 March and 23 September.
In the Southern Hemisphere, the opposite is true during the same period.
The Earth’s rotation and revolution together create day, night, and seasons.

quiz.q: What is the term for Earth turning around its own axis?
quiz.explain: Rotation is the motion of Earth around its axis.

quiz.q: Which line divides Earth into northern and southern hemispheres?
quiz.explain: The equator is the imaginary circle dividing the hemispheres.

quiz.q: How many hours are in one day?
quiz.explain: A day is divided into 24 hours.

quiz.q: What is the period of Earth’s revolution around the Sun?
quiz.explain: One year is about 365 days and 6 hours.

quiz.q: What is the name of the Moon’s phases when the illuminated part increases?
quiz.explain: Waxing phases occur when the illuminated part grows.

quiz.q: Which city is in the Northern Hemisphere?
quiz.explain: Kolkata is in the Northern Hemisphere.

quiz.q: What is a leap year?
quiz.explain: Leap year has 366 days, adding 29 Feb.

quiz.q: Which part of Earth faces the Sun during daytime?
options: The side facing the North Pole
quiz.explain: Daytime occurs when Earth faces the Sun.

quiz.q: What is the term for Earth’s motion around the Sun?
quiz.explain: Revolution is the motion around the Sun.

quiz.q: How many tithis are there in a lunar month?
quiz.explain: A lunar month has 15 waxing and 15 waning tithis.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: - Emotions are feelings that arise when something happens to us.
- Coping with emotions means understanding them and not letting them control us.
- Anger is a natural emotion but should be expressed calmly.
- Sadness, joy, fear, jealousy, and disappointment are all normal emotions.
- A balanced personality has good and bad traits; we should know both.
- Knowing our flaws helps us improve and become kinder.
- When we feel angry, we can pause, breathe, and think before reacting.
- We should not blame others for our feelings; we take responsibility.
- Expressing emotions in a reasonable way helps others understand us.
- A good attitude includes cooperation, listening, and respect.
- Being self‑aware helps us notice when we are too harsh or too kind.
- We can change bad habits by practicing better behaviour.
- A positive mindset encourages learning and growth.
- Respecting others’ feelings builds strong friendships and teamwork.
- Avoiding greed and jealousy leads to happier relationships.

quiz.q: Which emotion is described as a natural response when something does not go as we wish?
quiz.explain: Anger is the emotion that arises when things are not as desired.

quiz.q: What is the first step in coping with anger?
quiz.explain: Taking a deep breath helps calm the mind before reacting.

quiz.q: A balanced personality includes which of the following?
quiz.explain: A balanced personality has both strengths and weaknesses.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel jealous of a friend’s success?
quiz.explain: Talking helps you understand and manage jealousy.

quiz.q: Which action shows cooperation?
quiz.explain: Listening and helping are signs of cooperation.

quiz.q: When should you express anger?
quiz.explain: Anger should be expressed when you are upset, but calmly.

quiz.q: What is a harmful effect of uncontrolled anger?
quiz.explain: Uncontrolled anger can cause headaches and other health issues.

quiz.q: Which of these is a positive trait?
quiz.explain: Generosity is a positive trait.

quiz.q: What does coping with emotions help you avoid?
quiz.explain: Coping helps avoid misunderstandings and trouble.

quiz.q: If you know your flaw is being too talkative, what can you do?
quiz.explain: Listening more helps balance a talkative habit.

subject: EVS Part 1
chapter: Busy at Work – our Internal Organs
notes: Respiration is the process of breathing in oxygen and breathing out carbon dioxide.
The lungs are the main organs of respiration and are protected by the ribs.
The trachea (windpipe) carries air from the nose to the lungs.
The diaphragm is a muscle that moves up and down to help us breathe.
Air enters the lungs through the alveoli where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with blood.
Smoking introduces harmful particles that damage the lungs and can cause lung cancer.
The alimentary canal is a long tube from the mouth to the anus that digests food.
The stomach churns food into a moist mass called a bolus.
The small intestine absorbs most of the nutrients and water from food.
The large intestine absorbs remaining water and forms faeces.
Saliva contains enzymes that start digestion in the mouth and helps swallow food.
The heart pumps blood through the circulatory system, keeping oxygen and nutrients flowing.
The nervous system coordinates all body functions by sending signals through nerves.
The brain is the control centre of the nervous system.
The circulatory system includes the heart and blood vessels.
The respiratory, digestive, circulatory and nervous systems work together for life.
If one organ fails, the whole system can be affected.
Healthy habits like not smoking and eating slowly keep these systems working well.

quiz.q: Which organ is the main site where oxygen enters the blood?
quiz.explain: Oxygen enters the blood in the alveoli of the lungs.

quiz.q: What is the function of the diaphragm?
quiz.explain: The diaphragm moves up and down to allow air in and out of the lungs.

quiz.q: What does saliva do in the mouth?
quiz.explain: Saliva contains enzymes that begin the digestion of food.

quiz.q: Which system carries messages between the brain and body parts?
quiz.explain: The nervous system uses nerves to send signals.

quiz.q: What happens to the air after it passes through the alveoli?
options: It is stored in the lungs
It is exchanged for blood gases
quiz.explain: Oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves.

quiz.q: Why is smoking harmful to the lungs?
quiz.explain: Smoke contains toxins that damage lung tissue.

quiz.q: What is the main function of the small intestine?
quiz.explain: It absorbs most nutrients and water.

quiz.q: Which organ helps keep the blood moving?
quiz.explain: The heart pumps blood through vessels.

quiz.q: What is the term for the long tube that digests food?
quiz.explain: The alimentary canal runs from mouth to anus.

quiz.q: What is the role of the nervous system?
quiz.explain: It coordinates all bodily functions via nerves.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Growth is the increase in height and weight from birth to adulthood.
Physical growth stops around 18 years old for both boys and girls.
Development means learning new skills and becoming more efficient.
Infants start by crying, then learn to turn their head and smile.
Around 1 year they can feed themselves and hold objects.
By 2 years they can walk, run, and pick up small items.
Children develop coordination between different movements as they grow.
Learning a skill is called acquiring a new ability.
Practice makes a skill easier and reduces mistakes.
Malnutrition can stop a child from growing tall.
Good food, exercise, and positive thoughts help growth.
Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to children.
Children become independent when they can do tasks alone.
The more skills we learn, the less we depend on others.
Each person has a unique personality shaped by genetics and learning.

quiz.q: When does physical growth usually stop?
quiz.explain: Growth stops around 18 years old.

quiz.q: Which skill does a 1‑year‑old start to learn?
quiz.explain: At about 1 year, children can hold a spoon and feed themselves.

quiz.q: What does heredity mean?
quiz.explain: Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to children.

quiz.q: Which activity helps physical growth?
quiz.explain: Skipping rope is a physical activity that supports growth.

quiz.q: Malnutrition affects growth by:
quiz.explain: Malnutrition reduces a child's height.

quiz.q: At what age do children usually start walking?
quiz.explain: Most children start walking around 1 year.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a skill learned early?
quiz.explain: Singing is usually learned later.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of learning many skills?
quiz.explain: Learning many skills reduces dependence on others.

quiz.q: Which factor does NOT help growth?
quiz.explain: Negative thoughts do not help growth.

quiz.q: What does the story of the industrialist illustrate?
quiz.explain: It shows that hard work and good decisions lead to success.

subject: EVS Part 1
chapter: Infectious Diseases and how to Prevent them
notes: Infectious diseases are illnesses caused by tiny living things called micro‑organisms or germs.
Each disease has a specific germ that causes it – e.g., flu germs, typhoid germs, malaria parasites.
Germs can spread in four main ways: through the air, through water, through food, and by insect bites.
Air spread happens when a sick person coughs or sneezes and tiny droplets fall into the air. Others breathe them in.
Water spread occurs when germs from a sick person’s faeces get into rivers, wells or drinking water. Drinking or bathing in that water can make you sick.
Food spread happens when contaminated food is eaten – germs can stick to hands, utensils or flies that land on food.
Insects such as mosquitoes and flies can carry germs from one person to another or to food. Mosquito bites can spread malaria.
Direct contact spread happens when you touch the skin or clothes of a sick person with skin diseases like ringworm or scabies.
Preventing spread means keeping your mouth covered when you cough, washing hands, covering food, avoiding stagnant water, and keeping insects away.
Covering food stops flies and dust from touching it, reducing food poisoning.
Cleaning water with bleach or boiling it kills germs and makes it safe to drink.
Mosquito breeding sites are puddles or standing water; removing them stops malaria.
People with serious infections are isolated in special hospital wards to protect others.
Vaccination trains the body’s immune system to fight a specific germ, so you don’t get the disease when exposed.
Vaccines for diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus and polio are given to children at regular ages.
Public health programmes, like clean water supply and vaccination drives, help stop epidemics.
An epidemic is when many people in the same area get the same disease at the same time.
Micro‑organisms are tiny living things that can be bacteria, viruses or parasites.
Germs are also called microbes or pathogens.
Good hygiene, clean water, and vaccination are the best ways to keep a community healthy.
If you feel sick, stay home and tell a teacher or parent so you don’t spread germs to classmates.
Cover your mouth with a tissue or your elbow when you cough or sneeze.
Wash hands with soap for at least 20 seconds after using the toilet or before eating.
Avoid sharing clothes, towels or utensils with someone who is ill.
If you see a mosquito breeding site, throw away the water or cover it so mosquitoes cannot lay eggs.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a way germs spread?
quiz.explain: Eating a rainbow is not a mode of germ spread.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cough?
options: Cover your mouth with a tissue
Throw your tissue on the floor
Cover your mouth with your hand
quiz.explain: Covering the mouth stops droplets from spreading.

quiz.q: Why is boiling water important?
quiz.explain: Boiling kills germs that cause water‑borne diseases.

quiz.q: Which insect spreads malaria?
quiz.explain: Mosquitoes carry malaria parasites.

quiz.q: What is an epidemic?
options: A disease that spreads through food
Many people in the same area get the same disease at the same time
A disease that only affects animals
quiz.explain: An epidemic means many people get the same disease together.

quiz.q: Which disease is spread by touching the skin of a sick person?
quiz.explain: Ringworm spreads by direct skin contact.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see a puddle of water?
quiz.explain: Covering or removing stagnant water stops mosquito breeding.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is given orally?
quiz.explain: The polio vaccine is given by mouth.

quiz.q: Why should you keep food covered?
options: It stops flies and dust from touching it
quiz.explain: Covering food prevents insects and dust from contaminating it.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of vaccination?
options: To make you immune to a specific germ
To give you a cure for all diseases
To stop you from eating food
quiz.explain: Vaccination trains the immune system to fight a particular germ.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: All matter is made of tiny particles called atoms or molecules.
Substances can be in three states: solid, liquid, gas.
In a solid the particles are close together and vibrate in fixed positions.
In a liquid the particles are close but can slide past each other.
In a gas the particles are far apart and move freely.
When we write with chalk, tiny chalk particles stick to the board and come off when we wipe it.
Pounding or grinding turns a solid into a powder, which is many small particles.
Naphthalene balls release tiny particles that settle on clothes, making them smell of naphthalene.
Energy is the ability to do work. It can be stored in fuels like petrol, coal, or produced by sunlight, wind, or water.
When a fuel burns, chemical energy is released as heat, which can be converted into motion (kinetic energy).
The Sun, wind, and water are non‑exhaustible sources of energy.
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion; potential energy is stored energy.
Substances differ in properties such as hardness, colour, smell, and solubility.
Objects are made from substances and have definite shape and size.
The same substance can be used to make different objects (e.g., clay can make pots, bricks, statues).

quiz.q: Which state of matter has particles that are far apart and move freely?
quiz.explain: In a gas the particles are far apart and move freely.

quiz.q: What happens to chalk particles when you wipe the board?
quiz.explain: The chalk particles fall off the board when it is wiped.

quiz.q: When a fuel like petrol burns, what form of energy is released?
quiz.explain: Burning fuel releases energy in the form of heat.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a non‑exhaustible source of energy?
quiz.explain: Coal is a fossil fuel and is exhaustible.

quiz.q: What is the term for the energy of motion?
quiz.explain: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.

quiz.q: When you grind a piece of sugar, what do you get?
quiz.explain: Grinding turns a solid into a powder.

quiz.q: Which of these is a substance that can be found in solid, liquid, and gas states?
quiz.explain: Water exists as ice, liquid, and vapor.

quiz.q: What does the Sun produce that can be used to make electricity?
quiz.explain: The Sun provides both light and heat, which can be used to generate electricity.

quiz.q: Why do clothes smell of naphthalene after being stored with naphthalene balls?
options: The balls release tiny particles that settle on clothes
The clothes are made of naphthalene
The balls dissolve in the clothes
quiz.explain: Naphthalene balls release tiny particles that settle on clothes, giving them the smell.

quiz.q: What is the main source of energy for a thermal power station?
quiz.explain: Thermal power stations burn fuels like coal to produce heat and generate electricity.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Community health means protecting the health of all people in a community.
Good personal hygiene includes washing hands, brushing teeth and keeping clothes clean.
Nutritious food gives energy and strengthens the body.
Exercise and hobbies keep the mind and body active and happy.
Clean surroundings reduce chances of disease spread.
Spitting, littering and using old tyres can spread infections.
Safe drinking water and proper sanitation are essential for health.
Tobacco, alcohol and drugs are harmful habits that can lead to disease.
Addiction to tobacco causes mouth ulcers, cancers and other health problems.
Addiction to alcohol damages the liver, intestines and urinary bladder.
A wholesome life is achieved by good habits, avoiding bad habits and caring for health.
Community health is as important as personal health because a healthy community supports everyone.
Public toilets and clean roads help keep the community disease‑free.
Spitting in public places is a legal offence to prevent disease spread.
Good habits include informing family of your whereabouts, telling the truth and saying “No!” firmly.
Bad habits include chewing tobacco, smoking, biting nails and fiddling with objects.
Avoiding bad habits helps maintain personal and community health.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a threat to community health?
quiz.explain: Eating nutritious food improves health, not threatens it.

quiz.q: What is a legal offence mentioned to prevent disease spread?
quiz.explain: Spitting in public places is banned to stop disease spread.

quiz.q: Which habit can cause mouth ulcers and cancer?
quiz.explain: Chewing tobacco causes ulcers and cancer.

quiz.q: What does safe drinking water help with?
quiz.explain: Safe water prevents infections.

quiz.q: Which is a harmful addiction mentioned?
quiz.explain: Alcoholism is an addiction that harms health.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of exercising?
quiz.explain: Exercise improves mental health.

quiz.q: Which is a good habit for community health?
quiz.explain: Telling the truth is a good habit.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of liver damage in alcoholics?
quiz.explain: Alcohol consumption damages the liver.

quiz.q: Which action helps keep surroundings clean?
quiz.explain: Using public toilets keeps surroundings clean.

quiz.q: What is the effect of addiction to tobacco on the digestive organs?
quiz.explain: Tobacco addiction can cause cancers in digestive organs.

subject: EVS Part 1
chapter: The Earth and its Living World
notes: The Earth has four main spheres: lithosphere (land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (living things).
The lithosphere is the hard outer shell made of rock and soil. It is where we build houses and where tree roots grow.
The hydrosphere includes all water on Earth – oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater and ice.
The atmosphere is the air that surrounds Earth. It is made mainly of nitrogen, oxygen, water vapour and carbon dioxide.
The atmosphere has five layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, ionosphere and exosphere. The troposphere is the lowest layer where weather happens.
The troposphere extends up to about 13 km. Above it the air gets cooler. The stratosphere starts at about 13 km and contains the ozone layer.
The ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays from the sun. This protects living things.
The water cycle is a continuous loop: evaporation, condensation, clouds, precipitation (rain, snow) and runoff. It keeps water moving on Earth.
Evaporation happens when the sun heats water and it turns into vapour. It rises into the troposphere.
Condensation is when vapour cools and turns back into liquid droplets, forming clouds. When droplets become heavy they fall as rain or snow.

quiz.q: Which sphere of the Earth is the outermost layer that surrounds the planet?
quiz.explain: The atmosphere is the outermost gaseous envelope around Earth.

quiz.q: What is the layer of the atmosphere where most weather occurs?
quiz.explain: Weather phenomena like clouds and rain happen in the troposphere.

quiz.q: Which gas in the stratosphere protects life from harmful rays?
quiz.explain: Ozone absorbs ultraviolet rays from the Sun.

quiz.q: What is the main source of water for rivers?
quiz.explain: Rainfall and melting ice feed rivers.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a landform?
quiz.explain: River is a water body, not a landform.

quiz.q: What is the term for water that has fallen from clouds and lands on the ground?
quiz.explain: Precipitation includes rain, snow, etc.

quiz.q: Which sphere contains the Earth's crust?
quiz.explain: The lithosphere is the Earth's crust and upper mantle.

quiz.q: What is the main component of the Earth's atmosphere?
quiz.explain: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere.

quiz.q: Which process turns water vapor into liquid droplets in clouds?
quiz.explain: Condensation forms cloud droplets.

quiz.q: Which of these is a type of freshwater body?
quiz.explain: A lake is a freshwater body; oceans and seas are saltwater.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: - Biodiversity is the variety of living things in a particular area.
- Living things depend on each other and on non‑living factors like sunlight, air, water, and soil.
- A food chain shows who eats whom; each link is a species or group.
- A food web is a network of many food chains connected together.
- Plants are the base of most food chains because they make food using sunlight, water, and CO₂.
- Decomposition by micro‑organisms turns dead matter into nutrients for soil.
- The water cycle keeps water moving through evaporation, condensation and precipitation.
- The carbon cycle involves plants taking in CO₂ and releasing O₂, while animals breathe O₂ and exhale CO₂.
- Balance in the environment means that food, water, and nutrients are available for all living things.
- If one link in a food chain disappears, the whole chain can be affected.
- Scientists observe living things in different conditions (day/night, seasons) to study biodiversity.
- Observations may include noting shape, colour, sound, and habitat of organisms.
- A food chain can be broken if one link is removed; it then becomes a food web if many chains interconnect.
- Maintaining biodiversity helps keep ecosystems stable and productive.
- Human activities like using insecticides can harm beneficial insects and disrupt balance.
- Plants need nutrients from soil, which are replenished by decomposition and fertilisation.
- Oxygen produced by plants is essential for animal respiration.
- Micro‑organisms in soil help recycle nutrients and support plant growth.
- The environment is a system where living and non‑living factors interact and give and take.
- Conservation of habitats protects many species and keeps ecosystems functioning.
- Simple actions like planting trees, reducing waste, and protecting water bodies help maintain balance.

quiz.q: What is the base of most food chains?
quiz.explain: Plants produce food through photosynthesis, providing energy for other organisms.

quiz.q: Which cycle involves plants taking in CO₂ and releasing O₂?
quiz.explain: The carbon cycle describes this exchange.

quiz.q: If a predator disappears from a food chain, what may happen?
quiz.explain: Without the predator, prey may over‑populate, disrupting the chain.

quiz.q: What process turns dead plants and animals into soil nutrients?
quiz.explain: Decomposition by micro‑organisms breaks down organic matter.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a non‑living factor in the environment?
quiz.explain: Plants are living; the others are non‑living.

quiz.q: What does a food web represent?
options: All possible food chains in an ecosystem
quiz.explain: A food web shows many interconnected food chains.

quiz.q: Which organism is a primary producer?
quiz.explain: Plants (grass) produce food using sunlight.

quiz.q: Why are micro‑organisms important for soil?
quiz.explain: They break down matter, releasing nutrients.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the water cycle?
quiz.explain: It transports water through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about biodiversity?
options: It is the variety of living things in an area
It is unrelated to food chains
quiz.explain: Biodiversity refers to the variety of species in a place.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Family is a group where everyone has a role in decisions.
Each member’s opinion matters and should be heard before any choice.
We talk, listen, and agree together to make fair decisions.
Honesty is important in family and public life; it builds trust and efficiency.
Co‑operation means working together and sharing responsibilities.
Tolerance means accepting others’ differences and not judging them.
Gender equality means boys and girls, men and women are treated the same.
Everyone should help with household chores, not just one person.
When a mistake happens, we should admit it and correct it together.
Being honest and cooperative helps the family grow stronger and happier.

quiz.q: What should you do before making a decision in your family?
quiz.explain: All family members’ views are considered before deciding.

quiz.q: Why is honesty important in public life?
quiz.explain: Honesty helps public services run smoothly and efficiently.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of cooperation?
options: Only one person does all chores
quiz.explain: Cooperation means sharing tasks and supporting each other.

quiz.q: What does gender equality mean?
options: Boys and girls are treated the same
quiz.explain: Gender equality means treating boys and girls, men and women equally.

quiz.q: Tolerance helps us to:
quiz.explain: Tolerance means listening and understanding others’ views.

quiz.q: If a family member makes a mistake, the best action is to:
quiz.explain: Admitting and correcting mistakes builds trust.

quiz.q: Which activity shows cooperation?
quiz.explain: Helping in cooking involves working together.

quiz.q: When deciding on a trip, you should:
quiz.explain: All family members should give suggestions.

quiz.q: Honesty in public life helps to:
options: Avoid waste of time and money
quiz.explain: Honesty prevents wastage and improves services.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of being honest?
quiz.explain: Honesty increases trust and efficiency.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: - Rules are laws that everyone must follow.
- Natural laws (gravity, tides) never change, but human rules can change.
- Traffic rules keep roads safe and traffic moving smoothly.
- Social rules help people live together peacefully.
- Everyone, no matter who they are, must obey the same rules.
- Disobeying rules can lead to punishment or unfairness.
- Laws are made to protect people and the environment.
- Some customs (like untouchability) were banned by law.
- Education laws (free primary education) help everyone learn.
- Rules should be fair, equal and not discriminate.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a natural law that never changes?
quiz.explain: Gravity is a natural law that is constant.

quiz.q: Why do we need traffic rules?
quiz.explain: Traffic rules keep roads safe and traffic flowing.

quiz.q: Which rule is an example of a law that protects the environment?
options: Ban on dumping garbage in rivers
quiz.explain: Banning garbage dumping protects rivers.

quiz.q: What is an example of a social rule that was changed by law?
quiz.explain: Untouchability was banned by law.

quiz.q: Who can break the rules?
quiz.explain: Rules apply to everyone.

quiz.q: Which of these is a human-made rule that can change?
quiz.explain: Human rules like traffic rules can be changed.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of laws?
quiz.explain: Laws aim for equality and justice.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a natural law?
quiz.explain: Traffic rules are human-made.

quiz.q: Why was the voting age lowered from 21 to 18?
options: To give more people a voice
To stop young people from voting
quiz.explain: Lowering age gives more people a vote.

quiz.q: Which rule helps protect children?
quiz.explain: Banning child labour protects children.

subject: EVS Part 1
chapter: Let us Solve our own Problems
notes: Problems in civic life are issues that disturb the harmony of a community.
A problem is something that causes inconvenience or difficulty.
Disputes are problems that arise between people or groups.
Peacekeepers are people who help solve disputes peacefully.
The Mahatma Gandhi Dispute‑Free Village Mission helps villages solve their own problems.
In a village, people can solve problems by discussion, cooperation and participation.
If a problem is serious, it may need help from a court or a local body.
Cleaning a village through ‘shramdaan’ means everyone works voluntarily to keep the village clean.
Vermiculture is a method of using worms to turn garbage into manure.
Peaceful solutions include dialogue, mediation, and community meetings.
When everyone helps, problems disappear faster and society becomes stronger.
A peaceful family, school and society benefits everyone and helps progress in all fields.
The UN declared 21 September as International Peace Day to promote peace worldwide.
A group of peacekeepers can be formed in a school to help solve small disputes.
To solve a problem, first identify it, then discuss it with all parties involved.
The basic needs of all people must be met for a peaceful society: security, equality and participation.
Cleanliness, education and self‑reliance are essential for progress.
When you see a problem, don’t ignore it; act quickly to prevent it from getting worse.
A village can create a peace environment by setting rules, using peaceful methods and encouraging participation.

quiz.q: What is a problem in civic life?
quiz.explain: A problem is something that causes difficulty or inconvenience.

quiz.q: Who helps villages solve their own disputes in the Dispute‑Free Village Mission?
quiz.explain: Villages solve disputes through discussion among their own people.

quiz.q: What does ‘shramdaan’ mean?
quiz.explain: Shramdaan is voluntary work done by people to help the community.

quiz.q: Which method can help solve a dispute peacefully?
quiz.explain: Dialogue and discussion help resolve disputes without violence.

quiz.q: What is vermiculture used for?
quiz.explain: Vermiculture uses worms to convert waste into useful manure.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see a problem in your village?
options: Report it to a responsible person
quiz.explain: Reporting helps the problem be addressed quickly.

quiz.q: What is International Peace Day?
quiz.explain: It is a day to promote peace worldwide.

quiz.q: Why is cleanliness important for progress?
quiz.explain: Cleanliness supports health, education and development.

quiz.q: What is the main aim of the Mahatma Gandhi Dispute‑Free Village Mission?
quiz.explain: The mission aims to solve disputes peacefully in villages.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a way to solve a problem?
quiz.explain: Ignoring a problem makes it worse.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Public facilities are services or places that anyone can use, like schools, parks, libraries, hospitals, and transport.
Water, electricity, health, education and transport are the main public services that help everyone.
A school is a public facility where children learn and play; it is part of the community system.
Every child has a right to free primary education (ages 6‑14) and up to 18 for special needs (Right to Education Act).
Parents, teachers, and community members help build and run schools – they may donate money, materials or time.
Schools can organise cleanliness drives, poster competitions and play‑dramas to teach good habits to the village.
Parent‑Teacher Association (PTA) and Mata‑Palak Sangh (Mother‑Teacher Group) help parents and teachers cooperate for the school’s benefit.
A school’s unique features include its library, laboratory, playground, cafeteria, and special programmes like counselling or science clubs.
Students should identify all services available at their school and list them on a poster.
Public services must be used responsibly; misuse can harm the community.
The school is a part of the larger system of public services that keeps society running smoothly.
Children can become agents of cleanliness by organising drives and educating neighbours.
Community support for a school can include building classrooms, providing equipment or organising events.
Every child’s right to education is a fundamental right that must be protected by law.
Good school facilities encourage learning, health and safety for all students.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a public facility mentioned in the chapter?
quiz.explain: The chapter lists libraries, buses, and schools but not private gyms.

quiz.q: What is the main right that every child has according to the Right to Education Act?
quiz.explain: The Act guarantees free primary education for children aged 6‑14.

quiz.q: Who can help build and run a school?
quiz.explain: The chapter says parents, teachers and community members all help.

quiz.q: A school can organise a cleanliness drive to teach what?
quiz.explain: Cleanliness drives teach good habits and hygiene.

quiz.q: Which of these is a benefit of having a Parent‑Teacher Association?
options: Better cooperation between parents and teachers
quiz.explain: PTA improves cooperation between parents and teachers.

quiz.q: The Right to Education Act extends the age limit for special needs children to:
quiz.explain: Special needs children can study up to 18 years.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a public transport facility?
quiz.explain: Bus is a public transport facility; the others are private.

quiz.q: What should students do to identify their school’s unique features?
quiz.explain: The chapter suggests making a poster of the school’s features.

quiz.q: Which service is NOT listed as a public service in the chapter?
quiz.explain: Private tutoring is not a public service mentioned.

quiz.q: The school’s cleanliness drive helped the village to win which award?
quiz.explain: The chapter says the village won the Clean Village award.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: Maps show the shape and height of land.
Landforms are mountains, hills, valleys, plains, plateaus, islands, rivers, lakes, and forests.
Contour lines are curves that connect points of the same height on a map.
The space between contour lines is filled with colour in the layer‑tinting method.
Digital elevation models use satellite data to show height on a computer map.
Signs and symbols on a map are universal; e.g., a triangle for a fort, a circle for a lake, a dot for a village.
The key (legend) explains all signs and symbols used on a map.
Maps help in planning, military strategy, tourism, and environmental studies.
The height of the land is measured from sea level; negative values mean below sea level.
A map can show the same area in different ways: contour lines, colour shading, or digital elevation models.
When two maps are close together, the slope is steep; when far apart, the slope is gentle.
A hill’s cross‑section shows a gentle slope on one side and a steep slope on the other.
The Survey of India is the main map‑making institute in India.
Signs for common features: Post office (P), Hospital (H), Factory (F), Park (P), Playground (G), Road (R), Hill (H), River (R).
The colour used for water bodies is blue; higher elevations are light green or yellow, lower are dark green.
A map’s caption gives the title, scale, and date of the map.
The key is essential for understanding the map’s symbols and colours.
Maps are used in military operations, tourism, and regional development plans.
A contour line method shows unevenness; the layer‑tinting method shows height by colour; the digital method shows height by computer data.
The Survey of India started in 1767 and has made many accurate topographic maps.
A map’s symbols are miniature drawings of the objects they represent.
A map’s signs are simple geometric shapes or letters.
The height of a hill can be shown by a hill shading technique.
A map’s legend is also called a key.
When a map shows a wrong colour for a landform, it must be corrected.

quiz.q: Which method uses lines that connect points of the same height?
quiz.explain: Contour lines join points of equal elevation.

quiz.q: What colour is usually used to represent water bodies on a map?
quiz.explain: Blue is the standard colour for water.

quiz.q: The Survey of India was established in which year?
quiz.explain: The institute was founded in 1767.

quiz.q: Which symbol would you use for a fort on a map?
quiz.explain: A triangle is the conventional symbol for a fort.

quiz.q: What does a map’s key (legend) explain?
quiz.explain: The key shows meanings of symbols and colours.

quiz.q: In a layer‑tinting map, what does the colour of a space indicate?
quiz.explain: Colour indicates the height range of that area.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a landform?
quiz.explain: Post office is a man‑made structure, not a landform.

quiz.q: When two contour lines are close together on a map, what does that indicate?
quiz.explain: Close lines mean a steep slope.

quiz.q: Which method is the most modern for showing elevation?
quiz.explain: Digital elevation models use satellite data.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of using conventional signs on a map?
quiz.explain: Signs give precise information about features.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: सूर्य हा एक तारा आहे आणि तो पृथ्वीच्या जवळ आहे त्यामुळे तो मोठा दिसतो.
चंद्र हा पृथ्वीचा उपग्रह आहे आणि तो स्वतःभोवती फिरतो.
तारे हे स्वतः प्रकाश देणारे खगोलीय वस्तू आहेत, त्यांचा प्रकाश लुकलुकतो.
ग्रहांना स्वतःचा प्रकाश नसतो, ते सूर्याचा प्रकाश परावर्तित करतात.
सूर्यमालेत आठ ग्रह आहेत: बुध, शुक्र, पृथ्वी, मंगळ, गुरु, शनि, युरेनस, नेपच्यून.
सूर्यमालेत उपग्रह, लघुग्रह, बटुग्रह आणि इतर लहान वस्तूही आहेत.
बटुग्रह म्हणजे सूर्याभोवती फिरणारे लहान तारे, उदाहरणार्थ प्लुटो.
लघुग्रह पट्टा म्हणजे मंगळ व गुरु यांच्या दरम्यान असलेल्या असंख्य लहान खगोलीय वस्तूंचा पट्टा.
उपग्रह म्हणजे ग्रहाभोवती फिरणाऱ्या लहान वस्तू, उदाहरणार्थ चंद्र.
पृथ्वी व सूर्य यांच्यामधील ग्रह बुध आहे.
मंगळ ग्रहाच्या बाहेर असणारे ग्रह गुरु, शनि, युरेनस आणि नेपच्यून आहेत.
सूर्याच्या सर्वात जवळचा ग्रह बुध आहे.
सूर्यापासून सर्वात दूरचा ग्रह नेपच्यून आहे.
सूर्यमालेतील ग्रहांची क्रमवारी सूर्यापासून बाहेरच्या बाजूने: बुध, शुक्र, पृथ्वी, मंगळ, गुरु, शनि, युरेनस, नेपच्यून.
गुरुत्वाकर्षणामुळे सर्व वस्तू पृथ्वीवरच राहतात आणि अवकाशात जाण्यासाठी रॉकेटचा वापर होतो.
रॉकेटद्वारे अवकाशात जाण्यासाठी इंधन जाळून शक्ती निर्माण होते.
कृत्रिम उपग्रह पृथ्वीभोवती फिरून हवामान अंदाज, नकाशे तयार करणे, संदेशवहन यांसारखी कामे करतात.
अवकाश प्रक्षेपण तंत्रज्ञानाने भारताने चंद्रयान, मंगलयान यांसारखी यशस्वी मोहिमा केल्या आहेत.
अवकाशात जाण्यासाठी गुरुत्वाकर्षणाच्या विरुद्ध शक्तीची गरज असते.

quiz.q: सूर्य हा कोणत्या प्रकारचा खगोलीय वस्तू आहे?
quiz.explain: सूर्य एक तारा आहे.

quiz.q: पृथ्वीभोवती फिरणाऱ्या लहान वस्तूला काय म्हणतात?
quiz.explain: उपग्रह म्हणजे पृथ्वीभोवती फिरणारी लहान वस्तू.

quiz.q: खगोलीय वस्तूंचे प्रकाश स्वतःच्या प्रकाशावर अवलंबून असते, त्यांना काय म्हणतात?
quiz.explain: स्वयंप्रकाशित वस्तू तारे आहेत.

quiz.q: सूर्यमालेतील सर्वात दूरचा ग्रह कोणता आहे?
quiz.explain: नेपच्यून सूर्यापासून सर्वात दूर आहे.

quiz.q: ग्रहांना प्रकाश कोणाकडून मिळतो?
quiz.explain: ग्रहांना सूर्याचा प्रकाश मिळतो.

quiz.q: लघुग्रह पट्टा कोणत्या ग्रहांच्या दरम्यान आहे?
quiz.explain: मंगळ व गुरू यांच्या दरम्यान लघुग्रह पट्टा आहे.

quiz.q: उपग्रहांना कोणत्या ग्रहाभोवती फिरतात?
quiz.explain: उपग्रह सर्व ग्रहांच्या भोवती फिरतात.

quiz.q: सूर्यमालेत किती ग्रह आहेत?
quiz.explain: सूर्यमालेत 8 ग्रह आहेत (बुध, शुक्र, पृथ्वी, मंगळ, गुरु, शनि, युरेनस, नेपच्यून).

quiz.q: चंद्राच्या प्रकाशात बदल होतो, त्याला काय म्हणतात?
quiz.explain: चंद्राच्या प्रकाशित भागात होणारा बदल चंद्रचक्रण म्हणतात.

quiz.q: अवकाश प्रक्षेपणासाठी कोणते तंत्र वापरले जाते?
quiz.explain: रॉकेट तंत्र अवकाश प्रक्षेपणासाठी वापरले जाते.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: भारत हा एक विशाल देश आहे ज्यात विविध नद्या, पर्वत, पठारे, मैदाने आणि बेटे आहेत.
उत्तरेकडील सीमा हिमालय पर्वतांनी बनलेली आहे.
दक्षिणेकडील भागात अरबी समुद्र, बंगाल उपसागर आणि हिंदी महासागर आहेत.
भारताला तीन बाजूंनी पाण्याने वेढलेले आहे, त्यामुळे त्याला ‘द्वीपकल्प’ म्हणतात.
गंगा, यमुना, गोदावरी, नर्मदा, कावेरी या प्रमुख नद्या भारतात वाहतात.
हिमालयात उगम पावणाऱ्या नद्यांचा प्रवाह दक्षिणेकडे जातो.
पर्वतांमध्ये हिमालय, सह्याद्री, कोंकण आणि पश्चिम घाट आहेत.
पठारे म्हणजे उंच सपाट प्रदेश, जसे की थार वाळवंट आणि पश्चिम घाटातील पठारे.
भारताचे प्रमुख बेटसमूह लक्षद्वीप, अंदमान-निकोबार आणि कोकण बेट आहेत.
हवामान विविधतेमुळे वनस्पती, प्राणी आणि पिकेही विविध आहेत.
उत्तर भारतात गहू प्रमुख पिक, दक्षिण भारतात भात प्रमुख पिक.
मध्य भारतात ज्वारीचे उत्पादन जास्त.
राज्यांची क्षेत्रफळे वेगवेगळी आहेत – राजस्थान सर्वात मोठे, गोवा सर्वात लहान.
राज्यांची राजधान्या दिल्ली, मुंबई, चेन्नई, कोलकाता इत्यादी.
राज्यांमध्ये विविध भाषा, सण आणि परंपरा आहेत.
भारताचे भूगोल समजण्यासाठी नकाशा अभ्यासणे महत्त्वाचे आहे.

quiz.q: भारताच्या तीनही बाजूंस असलेल्या जलभागाला काय म्हणतात?
quiz.explain: भारताच्या तीनही बाजूंस पाण्याने व्यापलेला भाग 'भारतीय दूबीपकल्प' म्हणतात.

quiz.q: गंगा, नर्मदा, वैनगंगा, गोदावरी आणि कावेरी या नद्यांपैकी कोणती नदी हिमालयातून उगम पावते?
quiz.explain: गंगा नदी हिमालयातून उगम पावते.

quiz.q: भारताच्या मुख्य भूमीच्या दक्षिणेला असलेल्या बेटांना काय म्हणतात?
quiz.explain: अंदमान आणि निकोबार बेटे भारताच्या मुख्य भूमीच्या दक्षिणेला आहेत.

quiz.q: भारताच्या उत्तर भागात प्रमुख पीक काय आहे?
quiz.explain: उत्तर भारतात प्रमुख पीक गहू आहे.

quiz.q: भारतातील सर्वात मोठे राज्य कोणते?
quiz.explain: राजस्थान हे भारतातील सर्वात मोठे राज्य आहे.

quiz.q: भारताच्या प्रमुख नद्यांपैकी कोणती नदी सिंधू नदीला भेटते?
quiz.explain: सिंधू नदी स्वतःच एक प्रमुख नदी आहे.

quiz.q: भारताच्या तीनही बाजूंस असलेल्या जलभागाचे निरीक्षण करताना कोणत्या दिशेला पाणी वाहते?
quiz.explain: भारताच्या दक्षिणेला पाणी वाहते.

quiz.q: भारताच्या मुख्य भूमीच्या दक्षिणेला असलेल्या बेटांपैकी कोणते बेट अरबी समुद्रात आहे?
quiz.explain: लक्षद्वीप बेटे अरबी समुद्रात आहेत.

quiz.q: भारताच्या प्रमुख नद्यांपैकी कोणती नदी मध्य प्रदेशातून वाहते?
quiz.explain: साबरमती नदी मध्य प्रदेशातून वाहते.

quiz.q: भारताच्या प्रमुख नद्यांपैकी कोणती नदी दक्षिण भारतात भाताची शेतीसाठी महत्त्वाची आहे?
quiz.explain: गोदावरी नदी दक्षिण भारतात भाताच्या शेतीसाठी महत्त्वाची आहे.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: घर म्हणजे निवारा, अन्न, पाणी, वस्त्र व शिक्षणाची गरज पूर्ण करणारी जागा.
घराचे मुख्य घटक: दारे, खिडक्या, भिंती, छप्पर.
घराचे साहित्य: लाकूड, दगड, माती, चुनखडी, सिमेंट, विटा, काच, लोखंड, वाळू, कापूस.
प्रदेशानुसार घराची रचना बदलते – मैदानी, वाळवंटी, दलदलयुक्त, पर्वतीय, वाळबंटी प्रदेशांमध्ये भिन्न साहित्य व आकार वापरले जातात.
उष्णता, थंडी, वारा, पाऊस व ऊन यांपासून संरक्षण देणारे घर आपल्याला विश्रांती व सुरक्षितता देते.
अ, ब, क घरांचे फरक: आकार, साहित्य व रचना – जंगली प्राण्यांपासून संरक्षणासाठी ‘अ’ घर सर्वात सुरक्षित.
शहरी भागात ‘ब’ घर सर्वात जास्त वापरले जाते कारण ते समाजकंटकांपासून संरक्षण देते.
घर बांधताना नैसर्गिक साधनांचा वापर करून पर्यावरणपूरक घर बनवणे आवश्यक आहे.
बायोगॅस, पवनऊर्जा व सौरऊर्जा यांचा वापर करून ऊर्जा बचत करता येते.
पाण्याचा पुनर्वापर व टाकाऊ वस्तूंचा पुनर्वापर हे पर्यावरणपूरक घराचे महत्त्वाचे गुण आहेत.
घर बांधताना साहित्याची निवड व स्वच्छता राखणे हे प्रदूषण टाळण्यासाठी महत्त्वाचे आहे.
घर बांधताना स्थानिक हवामान व भूभागाचा विचार करून साहित्य व रचना ठरवली जाते.
घर बांधताना बेघर लोकांना निवारा देण्यासाठी शासन विविध योजना चालवते.
नैसर्गिक ऊर्जास्त्रोतांचा वापर वाढवून पर्यावरणाची हानी कमी करता येते.
घराचे डिझाइन व साहित्य हे स्थानिक उपलब्धतेवर अवलंबून असते.
घर बांधताना पर्यावरणपूरक साहित्य व तंत्रज्ञानाचा वापर केल्याने ऊर्जा व पाण्याची बचत होते.
घर बांधताना स्थानिक समुदायाची सहभागिता व जनजागृती आवश्यक आहे.
घर बांधताना वाळू, कोळसा, सिमेंट व विटा यांचा वापर होतो, परंतु पर्यावरणपूरक पर्याय निवडणे चांगले.
घर बांधताना मुख्य ४ साहित्य: लोखंड, सिमेंट, वाळू, विटा.
घर बांधताना आराम, रचना व हवामान या तीन गोष्टींचा विचार करावा.
घरातील सौरऊर्जेने चालणारी उपकरणे: दिवे, पंखे, पाणी पंप इत्यादी.
घर बांधताना पर्यावरणपूरक घराची प्रतिकृती तयार करणे हे शिक्षणाचे महत्त्वाचे कार्य आहे.
घर बांधताना स्थानिक नैसर्गिक साधनांचा वापर करून ऊर्जा व पाण्याची बचत करता येते.
घर बांधताना प्रदूषण टाळण्यासाठी स्वच्छता व पुनर्वापराचे उपाय अवलंबावेत.
घर बांधताना स्थानिक समुदायाची सहभागिता व जनजागृती आवश्यक आहे.

quiz.q: घराचे मुख्य घटक कोणते आहेत?
quiz.explain: घरात दारे, खिडक्या, भिंती व छप्पर हे मुख्य घटक असतात.

quiz.q: कोणते साहित्य घर बांधण्यासाठी सर्वाधिक वापरले जाते?
quiz.explain: सिमेंट हे घर बांधण्यासाठी सर्वाधिक वापरले जाणारे साहित्य आहे.

quiz.q: पर्वतीय प्रदेशात कोणते घर सर्वात योग्य ठरेल?
quiz.explain: धाब्याचे घर पर्वतीय प्रदेशात योग्य ठरते कारण ते उष्णतेपासून संरक्षण देते.

quiz.q: घराचे संरक्षण कोणत्या गोष्टींपासून करते?
quiz.explain: घर थंडी, ऊन, वारा व पाऊस यांपासून संरक्षण देते.

quiz.q: शहरी भागात कोणते घर सर्वाधिक वापरले जाते?
quiz.explain: शहरी भागात ‘ब’ घर सर्वाधिक वापरले जाते कारण ते समाजकंटकांपासून संरक्षण देते.

quiz.q: पर्यावरणपूरक घराचे वैशिष्ट्य कोणते नाही?
quiz.explain: पर्यावरणपूरक घरात कृत्रिम रंगांचा वापर टाळला जातो.

quiz.q: घर बांधताना मुख्य ४ साहित्य कोणते आहेत?
quiz.explain: लोखंड, सिमेंट, वाळू व विटा हे मुख्य साहित्य आहेत.

quiz.q: सौरऊर्जेने चालणारी उपकरणे कोणती?
quiz.explain: सौरऊर्जेने दिवे, पंखे व पाणी पंप चालवता येतात.

quiz.q: घर बांधताना प्रदूषण टाळण्यासाठी काय करावे?
quiz.explain: साहित्य स्वच्छ व पुनर्वापर केल्याने प्रदूषण कमी होते.

quiz.q: घर बांधताना स्थानिक समुदायाची सहभागिता का महत्त्वाची आहे?
quiz.explain: समुदायाची सहभागिता सामाजिक व पर्यावरणीय जागरूकता वाढवते.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: सर्वांसाठी अन्न म्हणजे आपल्या शरीराला आवश्यक असलेले पोषक तत्वे
वनस्पती सूर्यप्रकाश, पाणी, मातीतील खनिजे घेऊन अन्न तयार करतात
शेतीचे दोन प्रमुख हंगाम – खरीप (जून‑ऑक्टोबर) आणि रबी (ऑक्टोबर‑मार्च)
उन्हाळी पिके मार्च‑जून या काळात पेरली जातात
सुधारित बियाणे म्हणजे संशोधनाने बनवलेली बियाणे ज्यामुळे पिके जास्त आणि जलद वाढतात
सिंचनाच्या आधुनिक पद्धती – ठिबक सिंचन व तुषार सिंचन
ठिबक सिंचनात पाणी थेट मुळाजवळ पडते, ज्यामुळे पाण्याची बचत होते
तुषार सिंचनात पाण्याचे थेंब पिकांवर पडतात, उन्हाळी पिकांसाठी उपयुक्त
रासायनिक खते म्हणजे कृत्रिम खते, नैसर्गिक खते म्हणजे शेण, कंपोस्ट इ.
अन्नसाठा म्हणजे अन्नधान्याचे सुरक्षित साठवण, ज्यामुळे आपत्तीच्या वेळी अन्न उपलब्ध राहते
धान्य साठवताना कोरडे व हवा खेळती ठेवणे महत्त्वाचे
धान्य साठवण्यासाठी कडुनिंबाचा पाला किंवा इतर कीटकनाशके वापरली जातात
हरितक्रांतीने भारताला अन्नस्वावलंबी बनवले
सेंद्रिय शेतीत नैसर्गिक पदार्थ व खते वापरली जातात
शेतीसाठी पाणी मुख्यतः पावसाचे पाणी, नदी, तलाव व विहिरीतून मिळते
पाणी व खतांचा अतिवापर मातीची सुपीकता कमी करतो
कीड व रोगांपासून पिकांचे संरक्षण करण्यासाठी कीटकनाशके व रोगनाशके वापरली जातात
धान्य साठवताना बुरशी व कीड टाळण्यासाठी योग्य पद्धतींची गरज असते
शेतीत सुधारित तंत्रज्ञानामुळे पिकांचे उत्पादन व गुणवत्ता वाढते
अन्नसुरक्षा म्हणजे प्रत्येकाला पुरेसे व योग्य अन्न मिळणे

quiz.q: शेतीचे दोन प्रमुख हंगाम कोणते आहेत?
quiz.explain: भारतामध्ये शेतीचे प्रमुख हंगाम खरीप (जून‑ऑक्टोबर) आणि रबी (ऑक्टोबर‑मार्च) असे आहेत.

quiz.q: भातशेती कोणत्या हंगामात केली जाते?
quiz.explain: भातशेती दोन्ही हंगामात केली जाते, परंतु खरीप हंगामात पावसाचे पाणी उपलब्ध असते.

quiz.q: सिंचनाच्या आधुनिक पद्धतींमध्ये कोणती पद्धत पाण्याचा अपव्यय कमी करते?
quiz.explain: ठिबक सिंचन पद्धतीत पाणी थेट मुळापाशी पोहोचते, त्यामुळे पाण्याचा अपव्यय कमी होतो.

quiz.q: रासायनिक खतांचे मुख्य नुकसान काय आहे?
quiz.explain: रासायनिक खतांचा अतिवापर मातीचे क्षारपडणे आणि सुपीकता कमी होणे यास कारणीभूत ठरतो.

quiz.q: धान्य साठवताना कोणत्या गोष्टींची काळजी घ्यावी?
quiz.explain: धान्य साठवताना कोरडे व हवेतील हवा असणे आवश्यक आहे, अन्यथा बुरशी व कीड लागतात.

quiz.q: वनस्पतींच्या कोणत्या भागात अन्नसाठा होतो?
quiz.explain: कंद (उदा. बटाटे, कांदा) हे वनस्पतींचे अन्नसाठा करणारे भाग आहेत.

quiz.q: सुधारित बियाणे वापरण्याचे फायदे काय आहेत?
quiz.explain: सुधारित बियाणे किडी प्रतिरोधक, कमी पाण्यात वाढणारे आणि उच्च उत्पादन देणारे असतात.

quiz.q: पिकांचे संरक्षण करण्यासाठी कोणते औषध वापरतात?
quiz.explain: कडुनिंबाचा पाला पिकांवर फवारल्याने कीड व बुरशीपासून संरक्षण मिळते.

quiz.q: हरितक्रांतीचा मुख्य योगदानकर्ता कोण आहे?
quiz.explain: डॉ. एम. एस. स्वामीनाथन यांनी गहू व तांदळाच्या बियाण्यांमध्ये सुधारणा करून हरितक्रांतीला चालना दिली.

quiz.q: पिकांचे नुकसान टाळण्यासाठी कोणते उपाय केले पाहिजेत?
quiz.explain: कीडनाशक फवारणी व इतर संरक्षणात्मक उपाय पिकांचे नुकसान टाळतात.

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: अन्न टिकवणे म्हणजे अन्न खराब होऊ नये म्हणून केलेली पद्धती
वाळवणे – पाण्याचे प्रमाण कमी करून सूक्ष्मजीवांची वाढ थांबवणे
थंड करणे – फ्रिजमध्ये ठेवून ऊब कमी करणे, सूक्ष्मजीवांची वाढ मंदावणे
उकळणे – उकळत्या पाण्याने सूक्ष्मजीवांचा नाश करणे
हवाबंद डब्यात ठेवणे – हवा व पाण्याची प्रवेश रोखणे
परिरक्षक – साखर, मीठ, हिंग, व्हिनेगर इ. वापरून सूक्ष्मजीवांची वाढ रोखणे
लोणचं व मुरांबे – लिंबू, साखर, मीठ, तिखट घालून बनवलेले
बुरशी व किडे – अन्न खराब होण्याचे मुख्य कारण
सर्वात लवकर खराब होणारे पदार्थ – दूध, फळे, भाजीपाला
हिवाळ्यात अन्न जास्त काळ टिकते कारण ऊब कमी असते
उन्हाळ्यात वाळवलेल्या धान्ये व भाज्या वर्षभर टिकतात
उकळलेल्या अन्नात सूक्ष्मजीवांचा नाश होतो
फ्रिजमध्ये ठेवलेले अन्न ऊब कमी असल्याने जास्त काळ टिकते
मसाल्याचे पदार्थ वाळवून व पूड करून दीर्घकाळ साठवता येतात
अन्नपदार्थांची ताजेपणा तपासण्यासाठी सुगंध व रंग पाहा
अन्न खराब झाल्यास पोटदुखी, उलट्या, जुलाब होऊ शकतात

quiz.q: वाळवणे म्हणजे काय?
quiz.explain: वाळवण्यात अन्नातील पाणी कमी केले जाते

quiz.q: उकळणे अन्नाला कसे मदत करते?
quiz.explain: उकळल्याने सूक्ष्मजीवांचा नाश होतो

quiz.q: फ्रिजमध्ये अन्न ठेवणे का उपयुक्त?
quiz.explain: फ्रिजमध्ये ऊब कमी होते

quiz.q: लोणचं बनवताना कोणते घटक वापरतात?
quiz.explain: लोणच्यात साखर, मीठ, तिखट व लिंबू वापरतात

quiz.q: सर्वात लवकर खराब होणारे अन्न कोणते?
quiz.explain: दूध लवकर खराब होते

quiz.q: हवाबंद डब्यात अन्न ठेवण्याचे कारण काय?
quiz.explain: हवा व पाणी रोखण्यासाठी

quiz.q: बुरशी वाढण्याचे मुख्य कारण काय?
quiz.explain: पाणी व हवा बुरशी वाढवतात

quiz.q: मसाल्याचे पदार्थ वाळवून का साठवतात?
quiz.explain: वाळवणे दीर्घकाळ टिकवते

quiz.q: अन्न खराब झाल्यावर काय होऊ शकते?
quiz.explain: अन्न खराब झाल्यास पोटदुखी होऊ शकते

quiz.q: लोणचं व मुरांबे का बनवतात?
quiz.explain: साठवण्यासाठी लोणचं व मुरांबे बनवतात

subject: EVS Part 1
notes: वाहतूक म्हणजे एखाद्या ठिकाणाहून दुसऱ्या ठिकाणी जाणे किंवा वस्तू हलवणे.
विविध वाहतुकीची साधने: पायी, सायकल, मोटार, बस, ट्रक, विमान, जहाज इत्यादी.
पायी जाणे सर्वात स्वच्छ आणि आरोग्यदायी आहे, परंतु वेळ व श्रम जास्त लागतात.
सायकल चालवणे शारीरिक व्यायाम, इंधन खर्च नाही, प्रदूषण कमी.
मोटार, बस इत्यादींना इंधन लागते, धूर व आवाज होतो, ज्यामुळे हवा व आवाज प्रदूषण होते.
इंधन जळल्याने कार्बन मोनोऑक्साइड, नायट्रोजन डायऑक्साइड, सल्फर डायऑक्साइड व सूक्ष्मकण बाहेर पडतात.
हवेचे प्रदूषण श्वसनमार्ग व डोळ्यांना त्रास देते, वनस्पतींची वाढ कमी होते.
वाहतुकीचे चांगले परिणाम: वेळ व श्रमांची बचत, व्यापार वाढ, वस्तू व माहितीची जलद देवाणघेवाण.
वाहतुकीचे वाईट परिणाम: प्रदूषण, आवाज, वाहतूक कोंडी, अपघात.
प्रदूषण कमी करण्यासाठी: सार्वजनिक वाहतूक वापरा, CNG व सौरऊर्जेवर चालणारी वाहने वापरा, चालणे व सायकल चालवणे प्रोत्साहित करा.
वृक्षारोपण व वृक्ष लागवड केल्याने हवा शुद्ध होते व प्रदूषण कमी होते.
